title: Your chats on every device — round 3: connection, costs, what travels

steps.intro: Each statement restates one of your round-2 answers as a rule the design will follow. Mark any that misread you as Fails.

steps.path: Any chat seen from a second device
steps.headline: Everything a chat sends between devices is encrypted end to end. No server of ours can read it.
steps.changed: Stated from your pick: words, pasted files and notices travel locked so that only your own signed-in devices can open them.
steps.notice: Nothing changes on screen. If you lose every device, the server holds nothing readable to recover from; the git copy remains your backup.

steps.path: A chat with its host online
steps.headline: The host keeps running the chat. Other devices receive a synced copy and show it live. Switching moves the running part only.
steps.changed: Stated from your pick: no portable bundle and no container. The chat's files sync underneath; the live stream rides on top.
steps.notice: Switching hosts is quick because the new device already holds the chat. Only the pieces still being written need to catch up.

steps.path: Taking over a chat whose host is unreachable
steps.headline: When a chat moves hosts mid-reply, the unfinished reply is dropped on both devices. The old host discards its half when it returns.
steps.changed: Stated from your pick: discard, not archive, not ask.
steps.notice: You may see a reply vanish when you tap Continue here. Your last message stays, so you can resend it.

steps.path: Any chat hosted on the phone
steps.headline: The phone counts as a full host. The design assumes it will match the desktop; parity gaps are separate work.
steps.changed: Stated from your pick: no viewer-only phone mode. The notice before a switch names what the phone lacks today.
steps.notice: Until parity lands, a chat moved to the phone may lack the browser, documents and some helpers, and the notice will say so.

steps.headline: Every project appears on every device, as today. A chat can also open on a device that lacks its project folder.
steps.changed: Stated from your answer: no per-device project choice, plus a new way to open a chat for its history and feedback alone when the folder is absent.
steps.notice: Devices keep filling with every project. The chat-without-folder path is a new feature and gets its own question on page 4.

steps.path: Tapping the host chip toward a device missing the project
steps.headline: Before fetching a missing project, a confirmation shows what is missing, why it is needed and the storage it will take.
steps.changed: Stated from your answer: fetch then switch, never silently.
steps.notice: One extra confirmation appears only in this case. A device low on storage can decline and stay a viewer.

steps.path: A chat with more than one branch
steps.headline: Branches you forked on purpose are equals. Branches split by a network gap or a device move warn and offer to archive the older one.
steps.changed: Stated from your answer: the app records why a branch exists and treats the two reasons differently.
steps.notice: Deliberate forks sit side by side with no warnings. Accidental splits show a notice on the older branch with one Archive button.

steps.intro: Read the plain-words explainer first; it has the costs, prices and tradeoffs behind these four questions: docs/active/design/2026-11-07-mesh-sync/connection-options.md

steps.headline: Which path should carry a chat's live words between a user's devices?
steps.today: The phone can watch a desktop only over Tailscale, a separate app and account on every device. Our account service already gives each signed-in user a private room, which today passes only tiny change notices.
steps.problem: Tailscale leaves out most users. Our own server costs money and is a central piece, which sits badly with a fully open-source, self-hostable app.
steps.proposal: Pick one. The explainer's section 1 compares them in detail.

options.label: Through the account service, address changeable
pros: Sign in is the whole setup; works on any network.
Pennies per user; the server code is already open source, so a fork or a user can run their own copy and point the app at it.
Can hold undelivered words for a device that was asleep.
cons: A server stays in the picture by default; most users will use ours.
New work on the server and on every app platform.

options.label: Over Tailscale only
pros: Nothing of ours is required; our cost is zero.
Builds on the remote-access link that already exists.
cons: Every user installs Tailscale and signs in on each device; the phone's one VPN slot is taken.
No mailbox: a device that was asleep catches up only through the slow git upload.
Tailscale Inc. still runs a central coordination service.

options.label: Both, the app uses whichever is available
pros: Users who already run Tailscale keep working with no server of ours involved.
cons: Two systems to keep working and to test on four platforms; every bug has two causes to check.
Behaviour differs by path, such as the mailbox existing on one and not the other.

options.label: Direct between devices, introduced by the service
pros: The server carries almost nothing once two devices are connected.
cons: Still needs a server to introduce devices, and a relay for the one in ten networks where direct fails.
The hardest to build and debug, for a saving that is already pennies.

steps.headline: Should a device that was asleep get the words it missed from the server?
steps.today: Today a device that was off catches up when the host next uploads to git, which takes 10 to 30 seconds and never happens during the 2 to 5 seconds a sleeping computer allows.
steps.problem: Without a store on the server, a phone in a pocket learns nothing until the host is awake and connected again.
steps.proposal: Pick one. The explainer's section 2 explains why the sleep window stops mattering with a mailbox.

options.label: The server keeps undelivered words until each device collects them
pros: Every device catches up within seconds of waking, whatever the host is doing.
The host only needs to send a one-word going-to-sleep note.
cons: Encrypted words sit on the server until collected; storage is pennies but it is a copy outside your devices.
Needs a rule for how long to keep uncollected words.

options.label: No store; devices catch up through the git copy
pros: Nothing of a chat ever rests on our server.
cons: Minutes, not seconds, after a host wakes; a host that sleeps before uploading leaves the others behind.
The sleep gap from deck 2 stays unsolved.

steps.headline: Should a user be able to point the app at their own copy of the server?
steps.today: The app is built against one server address. The server code is open source, but nobody can tell the app to use another copy.
steps.problem: A fork, a company or a privacy-minded user cannot run the whole thing themselves.

options.label: A server address field in settings, ours by default
pros: Full self-hosting with one copied line; forks need no code change.
Keeps our server the default, so ordinary users notice nothing.
cons: Each device must be set to the same address; a mismatch looks like devices never connecting.
Sign-in and friends features would also move to that address.

options.label: Our server only; forks edit the code
pros: No new setting; nothing to misconfigure.
cons: Self-hosting means rebuilding the app, out of reach for most.

options.label: Decide after the live path works
pros: Keeps this round smaller.
cons: Hard to add cleanly afterwards if the address is assumed in many places.

steps.headline: Who pays for the live path on our server?
steps.today: Backup & Sync is free and the server already runs for about $5 a month. The app has no way to take payments. A donation page exists.
steps.problem: The live path adds roughly 2 cents a month per heavy user, so a thousand heavy users add $20 to $40 a month.

options.label: Free for everyone, we absorb it
pros: Nothing for users to understand or do.
The cost is small enough to carry for a long time.
cons: A sudden popular month lands on the company card; a cap per account (see deck 2) would bound it.

options.label: Free, with an occasional donation prompt
pros: Covers cost without accounts or tax work.
cons: Prompts annoy; most people never give.

options.label: Free now; a paid tier once there is something worth paying for
pros: Leaves the door open for a priced plan later.
cons: Building payments is a project of its own and does not change this design.

steps.intro: Section 3 of the explainer lists each piece with its measured size and what breaks without it.

steps.path: A chat with helpers, opened on a second device
steps.headline: When should the work of the assistant's helpers reach your other devices?
steps.today: Helpers' own transcripts sit beside the chat and never sync. On your desktop they are 8.4 GB across 327 chats, half your whole store.
steps.problem: Copying them everywhere multiplies storage on every device; skipping them leaves a helper's details empty when you expand them on another device.

options.label: Fetch a helper's transcript when you expand it
pros: Other devices store a few MB per chat you actually dig into, never 8 GB.
The chat itself reads identically; only the expand step waits a moment.
cons: Expanding a helper on a device that is offline shows a 'not fetched yet' notice.
A new host that needs a helper's details reads them a beat later.

options.label: Copy them everywhere, like the chat
pros: Every detail is present instantly on every device.
cons: Every device grows by the whole helper store; the phone would hold gigabytes it will rarely open.

options.label: Leave them on the device that made them
pros: Simplest and smallest.
cons: Helper details are gone for good when a chat moves hosts.

steps.path: Any chat, opened on a second device
steps.headline: Which smaller pieces should always travel with a chat?
steps.today: Only the chat file, its name, tags and handoff notes sync. Saved long outputs, pasted images, undo history, memory notes and plans stay on the device that made them.
steps.problem: A chat that moves hosts without them may show broken images, redo work it already did, or forget project habits.
steps.proposal: Pick every piece that should always travel. The explainer's table gives sizes.

options.label: Memory notes and plans (250 KB in total today)
pros: The assistant keeps its project habits and plans on every host.
Tiny.
cons: Memory keyed to a folder path needs translating when the project lives elsewhere.

options.label: Pasted images and dropped files (up to 32 MB each)
pros: No broken images when a chat opens elsewhere.
cons: A chat full of screenshots grows the sync by their size.

options.label: Saved long outputs (510 MB in total today)
pros: A new host can reread what the assistant saved instead of redoing it.
cons: A few MB per heavy chat.

options.label: Undo history (about 1 MB per chat)
pros: Undo of earlier edits works after a switch when the project sits in the same place.
cons: Useless where the project path differs; adds about 1 MB per chat.

steps.page: The phone, and chats without their folder
steps.intro: Sections 4 and 5 of the explainer have the details.

steps.path: A chat hosted on the phone, screen off
steps.headline: How should a phone-hosted chat behave when the screen is off?
steps.today: Nothing holds the phone awake during a reply. After the phone has been still and dark for a while, Android cuts the network for every app until the user picks it up.
steps.problem: A reply can stall mid-way when the screen locks, and a pocketed phone cannot host at all.
steps.proposal: Pick one. Google allows asking for a battery exemption only when the app's core function needs it.

options.label: Stay awake per reply, plus an opt-in setting to exempt the app from battery limits
pros: Replies finish with the screen off, no permission needed.
Users who host from the phone can opt in once, with the battery cost explained.
cons: Opted-in phones use more battery when hosting.
Still no promise in the deepest sleep without the opt-in.

options.label: Stay awake per reply only
pros: No permission prompts ever.
cons: A pocketed phone drops as host; viewers see 'host asleep' and may Continue here.

options.label: Ask for the battery exemption during setup
pros: Phone hosting works out of the box.
cons: A permission prompt before the user has seen any value; may be refused by Google's review.

steps.path: Opening a chat whose project folder is not on this device
steps.headline: How should a chat open on a device that lacks its project folder?
steps.today: It cannot. The resume browser refuses, so a chat you only want to read or ask about is stuck on its other device.
steps.problem: You sometimes need the context and feedback of a chat without caring whether the folder is here.
steps.proposal: Pick one. Each shows the fetch confirmation from S-6 as a way out.

options.label: Open in a temporary folder with a banner
pros: The assistant can talk, read the whole history and write notes into a temporary place.
The banner offers to fetch the real project any time.
cons: The assistant may try to read project files that are not there and report them missing.
Files written in the temporary place need a home when the project arrives.

options.label: Open to read and ask, no tools
pros: Nothing can go wrong; no stray files.
cons: The assistant cannot run or write anything until you fetch the project.

options.label: Always fetch the project first
pros: The chat always behaves normally once open.
cons: Waiting and storage for a folder you did not want; impossible on a full device.

steps.headline: Anything in the explainer that read wrong, or a rule you want written down?
steps.today: The explainer and this deck carry every fact the design will rest on.
steps.problem: A misread fact becomes a wrong rule.
steps.prompt: e.g. never store anything on a server, even encrypted
